title: What lies below the waterline of sustainable AI skills · hancrafted
description: When a task you keep explaining should become a skill, how to write its description as the moment you'd need it, what goes into the skill and what stays in project context, and what a shared skill needs to stay right: an owner, a version, tests and a retirement date.

Sharing it Midnight A shared skill needs an owner, a version, a review date Owner: Lab team · v1.3 · review March The card in the institute's fleet manual. metadata: owner, version, review date Surface the sea surface and the air above it Sunlit epipelagic Twilight mesopelagic Midnight bathypelagic Abyss abyssopelagic

Sharing it (1/3) Page 1 of 3 Shared skills are knowledge articles A shared skill needs an owner, a version and a review date, as Anthropic's enterprise guidance asks for every skill. Personal skill no header, only you run it Shared skill Control block Owner Lab team Version 1.3 Next review March metadata: owner: Lab team version: "1.3" next-review: March Collect sediment sample Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. 1 Hold the robot 2 m above the seabed … --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. --- Your AI Your agent runs version 1.3 version: "1.3" A colleague's AI A colleague's agent runs version 1.3 version: "1.3" Another team's AI Another team's agent runs version 1.3 version: "1.3" Owner Lab team owner Who fixes it when it breaks, and whom to ask when it goes wrong. “Team or individual responsible for maintenance”, in Anthropic's registry entry per skill. Version 1.3 version One author's edit changes what the AI does for everyone who runs it. Next review March next-review A date for its next review. Anthropic: “Skill authors should not be their own reviewers.” Personal skills skip this until you share them. 3 Third step: before sharing a skill, decide where the project details live, and give it an owner. In the story: Your notebook card, and the same card in the institute's fleet manual, like a company knowledge article. The Agent Skills format has no owner, version or review-date field; its optional metadata map holds them by convention.

Sharing it (2/3) Page 2 of 3 Who owns the shared skill library Shared, general skills need rules for who adds, checks and removes them, and there is no settled practice yet. Back to Slide 18: Who uses it, and where Shared · others too General use · used in any project care ●●●● Details kept beside, with an owner, a version and evals Owned, versioned and tested A plugin or managed settings Reaches a whole team: owner, version and evals before it ships. the fleet manual a plugin Front page of the shared skill library Shared, general use Before a skill goes in, beyond its owner and version Who may add it The organisation's library is set to “Requires review”, “Open” or “Off”; a reviewer approves a fixed version. Whoever can merge to the repository; for plugins, admins choose which marketplaces and plugins are allowed and enabled. Whom it reaches (its tier) fleet, ship or project Personal, shared, plugin or organisation-wide; only owners add or remove at the top tier. ~/.claude/skills/ you, in every project · .claude/skills/ the repository · a plugin or managed settings: a whole team. What it costs to load A loaded skill is a recurring token cost. The loaded SKILL.md stays in the context window: a recurring token cost. Which models and agents it works with which robots A skill's value depends on the model and the agent it runs in. Tested in the agent it ships to: the same model in another harness can turn a skill's effect around. When it retires Deprecate it when its evals keep failing or its workflow is retired. Pin production skills to a version; deprecate when evals consistently fail. SKILL.md , its metadata map --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Use when we reach a new site and need a sample … metadata: owner: survey-team version: "1.3" tier: organisation works-with: Claude Code, Codex retire-when: evals keep failing --- The Agent Skills format has no owner field; these keys are a convention. Not settled yet: no common practice so far. In the story: The fleet manual's front page. Fleet, ship and project are the tiers; the robots are the models and agents. Fleet, ship and project are this Episode's words, not vendor terms: vendors tier skills by audience and risk, not by how general the content is. Codex splits repository skill folders from user skill folders the same way Claude Code does.

Sharing it (3/3) Page 3 of 3 Does the skill make things better? Test a skill by running the same task with and without it, because a bad skill can do worse than none. Same task, twice “Take a sediment sample at a new site.” prompt: “Take a sediment sample at a new site.” Without the skill no skill: the baseline skill disabled: the baseline no card no card sediment stirred up Score · illustration 2 / 4 Held 2 m above the seabed Camera checked for loose sediment Core tube sealed Core over 30 cm With the skill the skill loaded collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md loaded 2 m skill · procedure card SKILL.md Score · illustration 3 / 4 Held 2 m above the seabed Camera checked for loose sediment Core tube sealed Core over 30 cm Test the description too Does the AI reach for the skill at the right moment? A few requests each way, near-misses included. The trigger set tests this line of the front matter: --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Takes a sediment core. Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. --- Should trigger the skill should_trigger: true “ Take a sediment sample at Site 7. ” “ Get a seabed sample here. ” “ New site: sample the sediment. ” Should not trigger the skill should_trigger: false “ Film the seabed at Site 7. ” “ Log yesterday's dive. ” “ Sample the water column here. ” near-miss The agentskills.io guide to descriptions suggests about 20 queries, 8 to 10 each way, each run about 3 times. Did you know? In one benchmark, skills an AI wrote for itself before solving the task, with no good run behind them, scored below having no skill. SkillsBench, 2026: 8.1 to 11.5 points below the no-skill baseline, in all three configurations tested. Of 98 public skills, 92 showed no significant effect; harmful ones lost up to 17.0 points. In the story: Two test dives in shallow water, the same task each time. Not Vercel's result: there, the skill tied no skill.

Keeping it alive Abyss Keeping a skill right costs you every month + Project details changed + A new tool arrived + A description overlaps another skill A card with a running tag, like a loan statement. Same in both views: the tag is the upkeep Surface the sea surface and the air above it Sunlit epipelagic Twilight mesopelagic Midnight bathypelagic Abyss abyssopelagic

Shared skills are knowledge articles A skill registry entry Anthropic's enterprise guidance says to keep a registry entry per skill with purpose, owner ("Team or individual responsible for maintenance"), version, dependencies and evaluation status including the last evaluation date 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com A skill review date is an adaptation Knowledge-Centered Service does not review on a schedule: "Let reuse of Not Validated articles be the review" 1 , and the page does not use the word "owner". Owner, version and a calendar review date combine KCS and Anthropic's guidance; no source defines them as a rule for skills. Sources (1) Consortium for Service Innovation, KCS v6 Practices Guide, Technique 5.2: KCS Article State ( opens in a new tab ) library.serviceinnovation.org The Agent Skills format has no owner field the Agent Skills format has no owner, version or review-date field; its optional metadata map holds them by convention 1 . Anthropic also says "Skill authors should not be their own reviewers" 2 . Sources (2) Agent Skills, Specification ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

Who owns the shared skill library Shared skills are tiered by audience Anthropic's tiers in claude.ai: personal skills, skills shared with individuals, group skills bundled in a plugin, and organisation-wide skills that only owners can add or remove 1 . "Fleet, ship, project" are the Episode's words, not vendor terms; vendors tier by audience and risk, not by how general the content is. Sources (1) Anthropic, Provision and manage skills for your organization ( opens in a new tab ) support.claude.com Who adds, reviews and removes shared skills the org library offers "Requires review", "Open" and "Off", a reviewer approves "a fixed version" and users stay on it until a new one is approved 1 . Anthropic says to pin production skills to a version and to deprecate skills whose evaluations consistently fail or whose workflow is retired 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Provision and manage skills for your organization ( opens in a new tab ) support.claude.com Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Token cost and model fit are per-skill facts a loaded skill is a recurring token cost 1 , and a skill's value depends on the model and harness it runs in 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Skill governance "still being worked out" is a judgement Anthropic's enterprise guidance lists what to track per skill (purpose, owner, version, evaluation status) and does not report how many organisations do so 1 , so the unsettled corner is the Episode's judgement, not a measured claim. Sources (1) Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

Does the skill make things better? Skills that score below no skill: SkillsBench, not Vercel skills written by the agent itself land 8.1 to 11.5 points below the no-skill baseline on all three configurations tested 1 . In Vercel's eval the skill tied the baseline at 53%; only sub-scores dipped (lint 89% against 95%, test 58% against 63%) 2 . Do not attribute "below no skill" to Vercel's headline. Sources (2) Li et al., SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals ( opens in a new tab ) vercel.com Bad skills can hurt, many do nothing of 98 public skills, 92 showed no statistically significant effect, and harmful ones lost up to 17.0 points by anchoring the agent on their own templates 1 . Curated skills raised the average pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5% 2 . Sources (2) Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Li et al., SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Test the skill's description too the trigger set in the agentskills.io guide to descriptions is "about 20 queries: 8-10 that should trigger and 8-10 that shouldn't", each run about 3 times 1 . Anthropic's guide says to build scenarios and compare against a no-skill baseline 2 . "Three and three" is in neither. Sources (2) Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Trigger tests in Google's Day 3: two sizes Day 3 says a description must pass checks "to hit the industry-standard 90% trigger accuracy rate", the first being "You must write 3 positive and 3 negative triggers", with no source for the rate. Elsewhere it says "Write three eval cases (two positive, one negative) before drafting the body" 1 . Its own counts disagree, it is Google's vendor guidance, and none of it is measured. Sources (1) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Skill evals in Google's Day 3: one figure misread Day 3 says "a skill stripped of its instructions scored 58%, while the agent without the skill scored 63%" 1 . In Vercel's post that is the default skill against the baseline on the test sub-score alone, and overall they tied at 53% 2 . Vercel's wording wins, and SkillsBench in the first note, not Day 3, is the evidence for skills scoring below no skill. Sources (2) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals ( opens in a new tab ) vercel.com

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:31 You are the captain Imagine you work with an AI model that is brilliant at its job, the most capable colleague you have. I will give it a picture, because we need one all the way down: you are the captain of a coastal research project, and the model is your pilot of ten years, who steers a diving robot on a cable from the control room on deck while you decide where the project goes next. 0:31 – 0:53 One settled condition Your pilot has one condition, and it never changes. He forms no new memories overnight, but he keeps everything he ever learnt as a pilot, every rule of the trade. That is an AI model: what it learnt in training stays, and what you told it in yesterday's conversation is gone.

What a skill is 0:00 – 0:23 Surface first We are still at the surface, so before we ask when to write a skill, let's see what a skill is made of. I'll use the words your chat app uses, and if you work with a coding agent, some Slides have a second view that shows you the files behind each part. 0:23 – 0:39 The mechanics, plainly I want to be exact about how a skill gets loaded, because everything later depends on it. So I say first what the AI really does, and use the dive only to make it easier to picture.

When to write one 0:00 – 0:14 Sunlight We are one level down, in the sunlit zone. Here we decide two things: when a task deserves a skill at all, and how to describe it so the model actually picks it. 0:14 – 0:31 Borrowed principles From here on I borrow principles from engineering, information architecture and UX, and they all lean on one idea: what works for people also works for AI. I say that as a strong rule of thumb, not as a law. 0:31 – 0:52 Why a rule of thumb It holds because the model acts only on what you hand it, like a capable newcomer on their first day. It is only a rule of thumb because there are places where it breaks, and I've put those in the notes on the next Slide for you to read.

The description 0:00 – 0:12 The label decides We are still in sunlight, and this is the part most people skip. A skill the model never picks helps nobody, so the description matters more than the instructions. 0:12 – 0:26 Name, description Before the model opens a skill, it sees two lines: the name and the description. That is all the index holds, and it is all the model has to decide with.

What context goes inside 0:00 – 0:13 Twilight Deeper now, into the twilight zone, where the light is dim. The skill is written and described, and the question is what context goes into it and what stays beside it. 0:13 – 0:28 A decision, not a law I want to be careful with the word rule here. Keeping the procedure apart from project details is a design decision with trade-offs on both sides, so I'll show you the trade-offs and you decide.

What context stays beside 0:00 – 0:15 Beside, not inside Now the other home: project details that stay outside the skill, in project files it reads when it runs. The procedure goes inside, and whatever changes from one project to the next stays beside. 0:15 – 0:29 Where it gets shared And who uses the skill decides how much care it needs. A skill for your own use can be loose, and a skill a colleague runs needs more, which sets up the next Section.

Sharing it 0:00 – 0:10 Midnight Now we are in deep water, the midnight zone. Everything so far was for you, so what changes when a colleague runs your skill? 0:10 – 0:22 Three jobs Three jobs wait down here. Give the skill an owner and a version, decide who looks after the shared library, and test that the skill actually helps.

Shared skills are knowledge articles 0:00 – 0:18 Your notebook A personal skill has no header at all, like a card in your own notebook. That is fine while it is only yours, because you know who wrote it, when you last used it, and who fixes it when it breaks. 0:18 – 0:42 Into the fleet manual Once you share it into your team's skill library, the fleet manual on our ship, it needs what any company knowledge article has: an owner, a version, and a date for its next review. It is the same skill with a control block on top, and your personal skills can skip this until you share them. 0:42 – 1:03 Why Why bother? Because once it is shared, one author's edit changes what the model does for everyone who runs it, and nobody knows whom to ask when it goes wrong. That is your third step: before you share a skill, decide where the project details live, and give it an owner.

Who owns the shared skill library 0:00 – 0:12 Back to the square Come back to the matrix, to the shared, general square. That is the kind of skill the most people rely on, so it is where care matters most. 0:12 – 0:36 What the front page needs A shared library needs rules beyond the owner and the version: who may add a skill, which tier it sits in and so whom it reaches, what it costs to load, which models and agents it works with, and when it retires. Each is a question somebody has to answer before the skill goes in. 0:36 – 0:55 The dark corner And then there are the questions nobody has settled yet. I want to be plain with you: I do not have the answers there, and I don't think many organisations do yet. If you have worked it out in yours, I would like to hear how.

Does the skill make things better? 0:00 – 0:21 Same task twice How do you know a skill helps? Run the same task twice, once without the skill and once with it, and compare the results, like two test dives in shallow water. Don't trust your feeling about it, because feeling useful and being useful are not the same thing. 0:21 – 0:37 The callout (pause) And this test matters more than it sounds, because a skill is not automatically a gain. A bad skill can leave the model worse off than no skill at all, which is the whole reason the comparison exists. 0:37 – 0:57 Test the label Test the description too. Take a few requests that should trigger the skill and a few that should not, and include near-misses, the ones that sound like the skill but need something else. Those show you whether the model reaches for it at the right moment.

Keeping it alive 0:00 – 0:09 The Abyss This is the deepest zone, the abyss, months later. Writing the skill was quick, and keeping it right is the work. 0:09 – 0:20 Nobody sees it Most people stop at the first good run, and the part below it gets little attention, which is why I want to spend three Slides here.
